nutshell: Most MOT/counting benchmarks and methods are built around urban video (people, vehicles) where appearance-based re-identification helps track association. CFC is a large sonar-video dataset (1,567 clips, 8,254 fish tracks, 516k boxes across 7 cameras/5 river locations in AK/WA) for detecting, tracking, and counting migrating fish, deliberately designed so appearance features are nearly useless (low-SNR, grayscale sonar) and so training/test locations differ - making it a benchmark specifically for detection/tracking/counting generalization rather than in-distribution accuracy.
contributions: A new large video dataset (1,567 clips, 527k annotated frames, 516k bounding boxes, 8,254 fish tracks from 7 sonar cameras across 5 river locations) - the first dataset to jointly support detection, tracking, AND counting annotations in a non-urban, non-RGB domain, larger than existing animal-tracking benchmarks.

A deliberate train/test split that isolates domain-generalization difficulty: training/validation data comes from a single camera location (KL), while four held-out test locations span a spectrum of distribution shift (new camera at the same site, new site on the same river, entirely different rivers/species).

A counting evaluation protocol (vertical line-of-interest crossing) and metric (nMAE normalized per-location, not per-clip) that directly mirrors the manual procedure used by real field fishery technicians, rather than adopting density-based crowd-counting metrics from prior video-counting work.

A tracking-by-detection baseline (YOLOv5 + SORT) plus an improved 'Baseline++' that adds two extra input channels (per-clip background-subtracted frame, frame-to-frame difference) - producing large generalization gains (e.g. reported -40.2% nMAE change at the hardest test location, KC) with only modest in-distribution gains - alongside an upper-bound ablation (Perfect Detector / Perfect Tracker Generalization / Oracle) isolating detector generalization, not the tracker, as the main bottleneck.
deficiencies: The paper's own upper-bound analysis (Fig. 5) shows that a Perfect Detector gets tracking/counting performance close to the Oracle at nearly every test location - meaning the tracker (SORT + LOI counting) is not the real bottleneck - yet the proposed fix (Baseline++) only changes the detector's input channels via a simple, dataset-specific heuristic (per-clip background averaging), which was never compared against alternative ways of improving detector generalization (e.g. stronger augmentation, different backbones, domain-adaptation techniques).

Even after Baseline++, the two hardest locations (KC and EL) remain far worse than the others, and the paper's own error breakdown shows EL suffers from a qualitatively different failure mode (undercounting from track loss/merges) than KC (overcounting from false positives) - the paper acknowledges 'generalization challenges remain' but does not quantify how much of the true Oracle-vs-Baseline++ gap is actually closed.

The entire generalization study is anchored to a single training location (KL) with a single held-out validation day out of 16 - there is no cross-validation across which location serves as the training source, so it's unclear how much of the reported generalization difficulty is specific to KL's particular hardware/river conditions versus a general property of the domain.

The reported Baseline vs. Baseline++ improvements (e.g. '-40.2% nMAE at KC', '+1.6 AP50') are given as summary numbers and scatter-plot comparisons in the main text, with the full numeric tables deferred to supplementary material - it's not fully clear from the main paper alone whether percentage changes like '-40.2%' are absolute percentage-point drops or relative reductions, which matters a great deal for an error metric already expressed as a percentage.
notable: The claim that appearance features don't help in this domain isn't just asserted - the authors trained an actual visual re-identification model and report it 'performed poorly' on their validation set, a directly-tested negative result backing the dataset's core motivating premise rather than an unverified assumption. Also notable: nMAE is deliberately normalized per-location rather than per-clip, specifically because clip lengths/fish densities are arbitrary artifacts of how continuous raw video was cut into short clips - a subtle metric-design choice that a naive counting-error implementation could easily get wrong, worth remembering when adapting this protocol to other video-counting problems.
